gate1.question: May this viewer see that this report EXISTS?
gate1.saysNothingAbout: which rows a viewer's predicate admits

gate2.question: Which rows does this viewer's predicate ADMIT?
gate2.shape: a predicate with a digest, resolved once per session
gate2.cannotBeFrontEnd: If the browser receives 60 rows and shows 8, the viewer has 60. Every dev-tools session would be a full-portfolio export. This is why the renderer rule forbids filtering in the browser.

twelveObligations: Expose a resolved scope predicate as a first-class SESSION artifact with a digest, not a role lookup at query time. A digest is what makes an audit possible.
Define scope CLASSES as an administrable concept. Per-user predicates do not survive the tenth user.

declaredAggregate.question: May this viewer read a figure DECLARED over a population wider than their predicate admits?
declaredAggregate.rule: A block whose source is a declared aggregate (`portfolio` and its sub-objects) requires an unrestricted predicate. Any narrower predicate means the published figure covers rows the viewer may not read.
declaredAggregate.neverSubstitute: Never re-aggregate the admitted rows under the declared figure's label. The sample of 60 projects is 12.7% of a 612-project programme and its quarterly variance has the opposite sign, so a re-aggregation is not a smaller version of the same answer -- it is a different answer wearing its name.
declaredAggregate.renders: You are entitled to this report. It publishes portfolio figures declared over the whole programme, and your data scope admits a subset of it, so those figures are not shown. This is the scope working, not a query returning nothing.
declaredAggregate.aggregateGrainIsNotThis: A scope class at `aggregate` grain has an unrestricted predicate and IS served these figures -- it just gets no detail rows. The two outcomes look similar on screen and have opposite causes.

projects.priority: Key Driver — Operational Performance · Treatment Capacity 3/4 · Risk score 4.0
projects.driverLong: Asset condition and treatment capacity — filter run times below design across twenty filters
scope: 1. Why this project exists

Dunmoor East is a 96 MGD conventional plant with twenty dual-media gravity filters, the oldest of which were placed in service in 1968 and none of which have had a full media and underdrain replacement. Filter run times have fallen from a design 72 hours to a measured average of 31 hours; unit filter run volume is below 5,000 gallons per square foot at three of the four filter batteries. Backwash water use has risen to 4.1 percent of production against a 2 percent design allowance. Two filters show media boil during backwash, indicating underdrain failure.

The consequence is a capacity constraint, not a water quality failure — finished water turbidity remains compliant because the plant reduces throughput to hold it. The programme restores rated capacity by replacing the media, underdrains and wash troughs in all twenty filters and rehabilitating the filter box structures.
2. The constraint that shapes everything

No more than five of the twenty filters — 25 percent of filtration capacity — may be out of service at any time, and none may be out of service between June 1 and September 15 beyond a single filter, because peak-season demand consumes the redundancy. Every commercial and schedule decision on this programme follows from that sentence.

It is why the work is phased into three construction contracts rather than one. It is why each phase is measured and paid by the filter rather than by lump sum. It is why the programme runs from 2023 to 2031 for work that would take twenty months if the plant could be taken offline. And it is why the single largest change order on the programme is a time extension: Phase 2 work slipped into the summer restriction window and had to be carried to the following construction season.
3. Physical scope, per filter

Removal and disposal of existing media and underdrain. Demolition of deteriorated concrete in the filter box and wall, repair of exposed reinforcement, and application of an NSF/ANSI 61 certified cementitious liner. Installation of a new Type S monolithic underdrain with integral media support, levelled to the manufacturer's tolerance. Placement of graded support gravel, 12 inches of silica sand and 18 inches of anthracite. Replacement of fibreglass wash troughs and the surface wash system. Replacement of filter influent, effluent, backwash and waste valves and their actuators. New filter-to-waste piping. Replacement of loss-of-head, turbidity and particle count instrumentation and integration into the plant SCADA system.
Plant-wide, the programme also replaces the two backwash supply pumps, the surface wash booster, and the filter gallery piping between the effluent header and the clearwell.
4. Contract packaging strategy

Three construction phases, competitively bid separately, each a unit-price contract with the filter as the unit of measure. Phase 1 covers Filters 1 through 6 and is complete. Phase 2 covers Filters 7 through 12 and is in construction. Phase 3, covering Filters 13 through 20, has not been awarded. It is a budget line of $15,900,000 with no contract behind it and no contractor named. That gap is real and is stated here rather than buried: 74.7 percent of this programme's revised baseline is committed and 25.3 percent is not.

Filter media and underdrains are owner-furnished under term supply agreements that span all three phases, so that every filter receives the same media specification and the same underdrain product regardless of which contractor installs it. Media is drawn down against the term agreement as each phase releases it.

Media acceptance is a laboratory test, not a delivery ticket. Every lot is sampled and sieve-analysed before placement, at the Owner's quality assurance consultant. One lot was rejected on effective size and uniformity coefficient. The credit for that rejection appears in the change-order log.
5. Delivery organisation
6. Budget and schedule position
7. Change history and the baseline movement
8. Risk register — live items

Filter floor levelness in the remaining filters. Three of the six Phase 2 filter floors were out of level beyond the underdrain manufacturer's tolerance and required a grout levelling course. The Phase 3 filters have not been surveyed. If the same proportion holds, Phase 3 carries an unbudgeted exposure of approximately $1.6 million. The Phase 3 bid schedule will carry a unit-price item for grout levelling by the square foot so that the risk is priced rather than negotiated.
Asbestos and lead in the remaining galleries. The north gallery contained asbestos-bearing gasket and pipe insulation. The south and west galleries are unsurveyed.

Phase 3 escalation. The Phase 3 budget line was set in 2023 dollars. Producer price movement in the intervening period on anthracite, stainless steel and site labour has not been reflected. Phase 3 is the largest single unpriced exposure on this programme.

Concrete deterioration beyond the allowance. Both awarded phases exceeded their structural repair allowances. The allowance basis for Phase 3 should be re-derived from Phase 1 and Phase 2 actuals rather than from the original condition assessment.

projects.name: Redmont Well Field Expansion and Raw Water Transmission
projects.driver: H&S Risk to Customer and Employee
projects.priority: Key Driver — H&S Risk to Customer and Employee · Risk score 4.0
projects.driverLong: Supply resilience — replacement of firm capacity lost to the Corvale River withdrawal curtailment
scope: 1. Why this project exists

The Redmont business unit takes 61 percent of its supply from the Corvale River under a withdrawal permit that was reduced by 14 MGD at its 2024 renewal to protect low-flow conditions. Redmont's firm capacity, defined as capacity with the largest source out of service, now falls below maximum day demand in eight of twelve months. The project restores firm capacity by developing six production wells in the Redmont Sand aquifer and connecting them to the Selby Point treatment plant.

The driver recorded at investment approval is health and safety risk to customer and employee, scored 4.0 and confirmed at regional review — a supply shortfall in a system serving 127,890 connections is a public health exposure, not a level-of-service preference. There is no regulatory deadline. That distinction matters commercially: the liquidated damages in the construction agreements are calibrated to the cost of purchased water during a delay, not to a penalty exposure.
2. Physical scope

Production wells. Six vertical gravel-packed production wells, each nominally 20-inch diameter with stainless steel wire-wrap screen set in the Redmont Sand between approximately 290 and 460 feet below grade, developed to a design yield of 2.4 MGD each and a combined firm yield of 12.0 MGD with the largest well out of service.

Well houses and pumping. Six masonry well houses, each with a vertical lineshaft turbine pump on a variable frequency drive, sodium hypochlorite feed for pre-disinfection, flow metering, water quality instrumentation and SCADA remote terminal units.

Raw water collection. Approximately 31,600 linear feet of 24-inch and 30-inch ductile iron raw water collection main from the six wellheads to the Selby Point plant, including two creek crossings by horizontal directional drill and one railroad crossing by jack-and-bore.
Electrical. Extension of three-phase distribution to five of the six well sites, one site served by a new 1,200 kVA pad-mounted transformer and dedicated feeder.
Site. Permanent access roads, wellhead protection area fencing, and stormwater controls at each of the six sites.
3. What is explicitly out of scope

Any treatment at the Selby Point plant beyond the existing train. Land and easement acquisition, which is carried by Northline's Real Estate group under a separate budget and is the principal schedule dependency described in §8. Decommissioning of the Corvale River intake, which remains in service at its reduced permitted withdrawal.
4. Contract packaging strategy

Well drilling is a separate prime contract, not a subcontract to the general contractor. Well drilling in Corvale requires a licensed water well contractor, carries its own bonding market, and is measured and paid by the foot against quantities that cannot be known before the test holes are drilled. It is therefore let as a separate unit-price prime under EJCDC C-521 and coordinated by the construction manager. The general construction prime, which builds the well houses, the collection main and the site work, holds no risk for what the drilling contractor finds underground.

The unit-price form is the substantive commercial decision on this project. Estimated quantities in the drilling contract's bid schedule are estimates only. The Engineer determines actual quantities and the Contract Price is the sum of the extended prices at the actual quantities. When the target zone at three of the six sites proved shallower than the test-hole programme indicated, the contract self-corrected downward. That is the largest single reason this project's baseline moved down rather than up — see §7.
Well pumps and drives are owner-furnished under a supply agreement and assigned to the general contractor for installation, on the same reasoning as any long-lead rotating equipment purchase.
5. Delivery organisation
6. Budget and schedule position
7. Change history and the baseline movement
8. Risk register — live items

Easement and right-of-way acquisition on the Selby corridor. This is the reason the project's end date moved from December 31, 2027 to December 31, 2028. Twelve parcels along the collection main alignment were still in negotiation when the general construction contract was awarded; four required condemnation proceedings. The construction agreement was extended by 274 days and the extended general conditions were paid. Three parcels remain outstanding on the northern segment.

Water quality at Wells 5 and 6. Iron and manganese in the step-drawdown samples at Well 5 exceeded the concentrations assumed in design. If sequestration is insufficient, greensand or oxidation-filtration treatment is required at the wellhead and is not in this budget.

Sand production after development. Well 3 produced above the 5 ppm limit through the first development cycle and required a second development pass. A screen slot revision on any remaining well would be a change to the drilling contract.

Plumbness and alignment. The specification requires the borehole to fall within a 10-inch circle over the screened interval. One borehole approached that limit. An abandonment and redrill is at the drilling contractor's cost under the specification, but carries schedule.

projects.name: PFAS Treatment Facility — Quarrydown Water Treatment Plant
projects.pmTitle: Senior Project Manager, Eastmoor Capital Delivery
projects.priority: CAPEX Priority Level 1 · Compliance Priority Level 1
projects.driverLong: Regulatory compliance — PFOA/PFOS maximum contaminant level
scope: 1. Why this project exists

Quarrydown Water Treatment Plant is a 38 MGD conventional surface water plant serving 164,871 connections across the Draycott business unit. Routine monitoring under the fifth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule returned perfluorooctanoic acid and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid in the raw water at concentrations above the maximum contaminant level of 4.0 parts per trillion established by the April 2024 national primary drinking water regulation for PFAS. The plant's existing conventional treatment train — coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation and dual-media filtration — provides no meaningful removal of either compound.

The project therefore adds a granular activated carbon adsorption facility downstream of filtration and upstream of disinfection. It is a compliance project. It does not increase plant capacity, does not improve any other water quality parameter, and would not be undertaken on asset-condition or level-of-service grounds. The compliance date driving the schedule is April 26, 2029.

A federal rulemaking proposed in May 2026 would extend the compliance date for PFOA and PFOS to April 26, 2031 and rescind the regulation of four other PFAS compounds. That rulemaking is proposed and not final; a petition for review of the underlying rule remains pending. Northline's position, recorded at the Level 04 investment approval, is that the project proceeds against the promulgated 2029 date and that the proposed extension is treated as schedule relief if it is finalised, never as a basis for deferral.
2. Physical scope

Adsorption facility. A new 21,400 square foot GAC contactor building housing twelve 12-foot diameter ASME Section VIII Division 1 carbon steel pressure vessels, NSF/ANSI 61 certified and lined, each holding 40,000 pounds of virgin bituminous granular activated carbon. Vessels are piped in six lead-lag pairs. Empty bed contact time is 10 minutes per vessel and 20 minutes per pair at the design flow of 38 MGD, with one pair out of service for changeout.

Hydraulics. An intermediate transfer pump station of four 750 hp vertical turbine pumps on variable frequency drives, taking suction from a new 1.1 million gallon filtered water transfer basin and discharging through the contactors to the existing clearwell.

Carbon handling. A truck-accessible media transfer bay, carbon slurry eductor system, spent carbon settling tank, and a dedicated backwash return line routed to the head of the plant through a spent-media isolation valve.

Yard and site. Approximately 2,900 linear feet of 42-inch and 36-inch ductile iron process yard piping, site electrical duct bank, a 2,500 kW standby generator pad, stormwater management for 4.1 acres of new impervious area, and reconstruction of the plant's north access road for carbon delivery loading.

Electrical and instrumentation. A new 4,160 V switchgear lineup, two 2,500 kVA unit substations, motor control centres, and integration of the adsorption facility into the plant SCADA system including differential pressure, flow, and online total organic carbon instrumentation at each vessel inlet and outlet.
3. What is explicitly out of scope

Replacement or rehabilitation of the existing filters, clarifiers or clearwell. Any treatment for PFAS compounds other than PFOA and PFOS. Residuals handling beyond the spent-carbon settling tank. Treatment of the plant's residuals stream, which is carried separately and is a known forward risk (see §8). Distribution system work of any kind.
4. Contract packaging strategy
The work is packaged into five agreements plus an owner-held contingency. Two features of that packaging are deliberate and drive the commercial risk allocation.

The pressure vessels and the initial carbon fill are owner-furnished. Quoted fabrication lead times for ASME/NSF 61 vessels of this diameter ran 44 to 52 weeks at the time of design completion. Procuring them through the general contractor would have put the critical path behind the construction award. They are purchased directly by Northline under a separate supply agreement and assigned to the general contractor for receipt, setting and installation. The consequence is that delivery risk sits with the Owner. A late vessel is an Owner-caused delay and is compensable to the general contractor. That exposure materialised — see the change-order log in §7.

The design engineer is retained under a separate professional services agreement and acts as Owner's representative during construction under EJCDC C-700 Article 10. The construction manager is a third party and does not carry design authority.
5. Delivery organisation
6. Budget and schedule position
7. Change history and the baseline movement
8. Risk register — live items

Backwash return PFAS loading. The plant returns filter backwash to the head of the works. If PFOA/PFOS concentrate in that return the contactors will see a higher influent load than design, shortening bed life. Sampling is underway. If confirmed, a separate residuals project is required and is not in this budget.

Early lag-vessel breakthrough during acceptance testing. A comparable facility detected breakthrough approximately ten months after startup. The acceptance test is 21 consecutive days at design flow; it will not detect a bed-life shortfall. The first changeout is an operating cost, not a capital cost, and is not in this budget.

Compliance-date ambiguity. If the proposed extension to 2031 is finalised, the separate liquidated damage tied to the compliance date in the general construction agreement becomes inoperative and the Owner will be asked to release it by change order. That is a credit exposure, not a cost exposure.

American Iron and Steel / Build America, Buy America conformance. Two vessels were rejected at delivery for undocumented plate origin. The remaining ten carry certified material test reports. The supply agreement was amended to require mill certification at shipment rather than at delivery.

projects.name: Westbrook Lead Service Line Replacement Programme
projects.inServiceValueBasis: Inception-to-date actual at the recorded in-service date. Not a GL capitalised value: capitalisation is carried on five of the sixty projects in this fixture and a calendar drawn on it would be mostly holes.
vendors: Sable Creek Public Health Associates, LLC
projects.driverLong: Regulatory compliance — Lead and Copper Rule Improvements replacement mandate
scope: 1. Why this project exists

The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, effective December 29, 2024, require water systems to replace all lead service lines and all galvanized lines requiring replacement by December 31, 2037, to lower the lead action level from 15 to 10 micrograms per litre, and to maintain a validated service line inventory. Service lines of unknown material are treated as lead until identified. Westbrook's validated inventory identifies 6,269 service connections requiring replacement or verification within the Marlow Creek business unit.

This is a blanket programme, not a project. It has no single design, no single site and no single completion. It is an annual production line measured in services replaced, and every commercial and reporting decision in this document follows from that.
2. Scope of a single replacement

A full replacement removes and replaces the entire service line from the water main to the customer's meter or first fitting inside the building, in one operation, and includes: documented right-of-entry attempts and their logging; permits; material validation at the curb stop by test pit or vacuum excavation; utility mark-outs; excavation and pavement removal; installation of new copper service line, new corporation stop, new curb stop and curb box; reconnection inside the building by a licensed plumber; restoration of the ground bond where a metallic service line was the electrical ground; flushing and a post-replacement water quality sample; issue of a pitcher filter and six months of replacement cartridges; GPS capture of the corporation stop, curb stop and building entry point; photographic closeout; temporary trench patch; and final restoration.

The unit price is not earned until all of that is done. A partial replacement — public side only, private side deferred — is a separate and lower-value bid item, and Northline's programme rule is that a partial is performed only where the customer has refused or failed to provide access after the reasonable-effort standard has been met.
3. Access is the binding constraint, not cost

The rule's reasonable-effort standard is four documented contact attempts using at least two different communication methods. After that the system is not required to replace the private side, but the obligation restarts on change of ownership. In this programme's experience the governing failure is non-response, not refusal — customers who never answer, not customers who say no.

That has a direct commercial consequence, visible in the change-order log: 412 services on Contract 25-2 were closed as Access Not Provided after the four attempts, generating a credit for the per-service items not performed, while the paid Test Pit at Curb Stop and Access Not Provided administrative items were still earned. Work was performed and paid for on services that were not replaced. Any reading of this programme's productivity that divides cost by services replaced will be wrong for that reason.

The second driver is geographic scatter. Block-wide replacement is materially cheaper per service than reactive replacement scattered across a business unit, because mobilisation, traffic control, mark-outs and restoration all amortise across the block. Northline's programme rule is that no fewer than 70 percent of each contract's services must be released in block-wide work orders.
4. Contract packaging strategy

The programme is delivered through a serialised family of annual unit-price contracts, not through one master agreement with task orders. Each contract is competitively bid, carries the same bid schedule, and is assigned a geographic sector and an estimated-quantity target list that Northline updates from the service line inventory. Contracts run concurrently. The numbering — 23-1, 25-2, 26-3 — is the year of award and the sequence, and it is how every commitment, invoice and productivity figure in this programme is keyed.

The reason for the serialised form rather than a single long contract is that unit prices for this work do not hold. Prices are firm within a contract year; each successive contract is re-bid to the market.

Restoration is a separate prime. Final paving cannot be placed sooner than 45 days after backfill, and work backfilled after the asphalt plants close is hot-patched and paved the following spring. A rolling programme therefore always carries an open restoration tail behind the replacement crews, and holding that tail inside the replacement contracts would make every contract's completion date meaningless. Restoration is let as its own term contract with its own five-year warranty.

The private side is performed by a licensed plumbing contractor under a separate term contract, because Ardenia plumbing law does not permit a utility contractor to make the connection inside a building.
5. Delivery organisation
6. Budget and schedule position
7. Change history and why the baseline did not move
8. Risk register — live items

Participation. The federal impact analysis assumes half of property owners will be unwilling or unable to pay a cost share. Northline does not charge a customer cost share on this programme, which is the single strongest lever on participation, but non-response remains the limiting factor and drives the Access Not Provided item.

Change of ownership restarting the obligation. Every service closed as Access Not Provided returns to the work list when the property changes hands. This programme's tail extends past its nominal completion for that reason alone.

Ground bonding. Replacing a metallic service line can sever a building's electrical ground. Restoration of the bond is in the plumbing contract, but a property with a defective pre-existing ground becomes a customer-property electrical issue Northline cannot resolve under this programme.

Pavement moratoriums. Streets paved within the municipality's five-year moratorium require full-lane or curb-to-curb restoration plus a non-refundable pavement degradation fee. That exposure produced change order CO-003 and is not fully mapped for the remaining sectors.

Unknown-material services. A service that pothole-verifies as copper leaves the replacement scope but has already consumed a paid test pit. A service that verifies as galvanized-requiring-replacement enters scope. The net of those two movements is the largest single quantity risk on every contract in this family.

projects.name: Selby Point Water Main Replacement Programme
projects.inServiceValueBasis: Inception-to-date actual at the recorded in-service date. Not a GL capitalised value: capitalisation is carried on five of the sixty projects in this fixture and a calendar drawn on it would be mostly holes.
projects.priority: Asset Risk Not Applicable · Good Performance
projects.driverLong: Asset renewal — break rate and hydraulic capacity on unlined cast iron
scope: 1. Why this project exists

The Selby Point distribution system contains approximately 58 miles of unlined cast iron main installed between 1922 and 1961. Break rate across that population has reached 34 breaks per 100 miles per year against a network average of 11. Tuberculation has reduced effective internal diameter on the 6-inch and 8-inch mains to the point that four hydrant districts cannot meet the fire flow committed to the municipality under the 2019 franchise agreement — which is why this programme's compliance driver is recorded as committed to third party rather than a regulatory mandate.

The programme replaces the worst-performing mains on a rolling basis, prioritised annually by a composite of break history, fire flow deficiency, soil corrosivity and coincidence with municipal paving programmes.
2. Scope of the annual work programme

Replacement of 6-inch and 8-inch unlined cast iron with 8-inch and 12-inch AWWA C900 PVC or ductile iron; new gate valves at every branch and at maximum 800-foot spacing; new hydrants and hydrant laterals; transfer of every service connection on the replaced segment, including new corporation stops and, where the existing service is lead or galvanized, replacement of the full service line in coordination with the lead programme; tie-ins to the existing network; abandonment and grouting of the retired main; disinfection, pressure testing and bacteriological clearance under AWWA C651; and full trench and pavement restoration.

Subsurface utility engineering — designating and test-hole locating of existing utilities to ASCE 38 Quality Level B and A — is performed ahead of design on every segment, under the design agreement, and is the single highest-value risk reduction on the programme.
3. Contract packaging strategy

Two geographic replacement contracts and two specialty term contracts. Contract WM-23-A covers the northern half of the business unit and WM-26-B the southern half; both are unit-price contracts with the linear foot, the each and the square yard as the units of measure. Both were competitively bid against the same bid schedule.

Trenchless replacement is a separate specialty term contract. Pipe bursting on runs over 40 feet costs materially less than open cut once restoration is counted, but it requires a specialist contractor, a different insurance profile and different means and methods. Holding it inside the open-cut contracts would have meant either paying an open-cut contractor's subcontract markup on it or not using it at all.

The conversion of footage from open cut to trenchless is the reason this programme's baseline moved down. 4,180 linear feet on the WM-23-A alignment was reassigned to the trenchless contract after the subsurface utility engineering established adequate clearance. The credit taken against WM-23-A exceeded the addition to the trenchless contract by $762,000, a 31 percent saving on the converted footage. Two change orders in opposite directions, one net effect — and a reading of either contract alone would show the wrong picture. See §7.

Restoration is a separate prime for the same reason as in the lead programme: final paving lags backfill by at least 45 days and by a full season across the winter, so restoration cannot govern a replacement contract's completion.
4. Delivery organisation
5. Budget and schedule position
6. Change history and the baseline movement
7. Risk register — live items

Utility conflicts at tie-in. Unmarked private services and a mis-plotted 4-inch gas main at fourteen tie-in locations produced change order CO-003. Subsurface utility engineering to Quality Level A at every tie-in, rather than at sampled locations, is the mitigation and has been added to the design agreement's ongoing scope.
Rock below invert. 2,340 CY encountered on Marlow Ridge Road against an estimate of 600 CY. The remaining southern alignment crosses the same formation and is not fully characterised.

Pavement moratoriums and restoration escalation. The municipality's five-year utility-cut moratorium and rising asphalt unit prices are the largest cost pressure on the restoration term contract. Unit prices escalate at each annual renewal by a factor of 1.03, which has been below actual market movement in two of the last three renewals.

Seasonal restoration tail. Work backfilled after the asphalt plants close carries retainage and the restoration holdback across the winter. That is a working-capital effect on the contractor and a reporting effect on Northline: committed value is earned but not paid, and the programme's in-service dates lag its construction completion.

legend.runtime: RUNTIME SOURCES DO NOT APPEAR HERE. Correspondence read at question time produces an OBSERVATION, which resolves against these nodes and is shown in the evidence panel. There is no Email node, no Message node and no Observation node, and there must never be one: permissions follow the source, not the subject, so a message about a project is not readable by everyone who can read the project. nodes.note: NEW, and CORRECTED August 5, 2026 -- it was 'Forecast Snapshot' with three monthly calendarizations, which is not a cadence this customer runs. The version column carries two chains, not one: three plan adoptions (MTP 2024, 2025, 2026), successive within a plan horizon, and three fiscal-year cuts (3+9, 6+6, 9+3), successive within a fiscal year. Both are `issued` -- nothing approves either -- so neither has an `active` member and a validator applying the approval chain's one-active rule would fail every well-formed row here. m_budget.reading: Read the approved plan amount for each project the viewer's scope admits.

m_forecast.reading: Read the forecast for each project, then name which cut of which fiscal year it was issued at.

m_mtp.reading: Read the adopted mid-term plan for the declared horizon at the adoption the selector resolves to, and name the adoption. The walk stops at the horizon boundary: an adoption stating a different horizon is a different chain, not an earlier member of this one.

m_authorized.reading: Take every approval row for the project, keep the one with the most recent approval date, and read its amount.

m_committed.reading: Add up the open purchase orders raised against the project.

m_actual.reading: Add up the general-ledger lines posted to the project.

m_cwip.reading: Read the project's construction-work-in-progress balance at period end.

m_capitalized.reading: Follow the project's CWIP through to the assets it became, and add up what transferred.

m_rate_base.reading: Follow capital through to in-service assets, then to the commission that admits them to rate base.

m_eac.reading: Read the full-span forecast for the project at the latest cut of the fiscal year, and name the cut.

m_eac_variance.reading: Subtract the approved budget from the full-span forecast. This crosses two bases by declaration, because the subtraction is the measure's whole meaning.

m_eac_variance_pct.reading: Express the EAC variance as a share of the approved budget.

m_gap.reading: Across the whole programme, subtract approved budget from forecast over the five-year horizon.

m_gap_pct.reading: Express the programme gap as a share of approved budget.

m_plan_period.reading: Read the calendarised plan for the single period asked about.

m_variance_period.reading: Subtract the period plan from posted spend for the same period. Negative is underspend.

m_variance_pct.reading: Express plan-to-actual variance as a share of plan.

m_contingency_alloc.reading: Read the contingency held against the project at its current authorisation.

m_contingency_used.reading: Add up the posted spend charged to the project's contingency account since inception.

m_pct_complete.reading: Read physical completion for each project, and when combining projects weight by budget rather than averaging.

m_schedule_variance.reading: Compare the project's forecast in-service date with its planned one.

m_cwip_age.reading: Read how long the project's CWIP balance has been held without transfer.

m_pis_value.reading: Add up capital scheduled or recorded as placed in service in the window, and label each month's basis.

vintage.label: Plan adoption

unsupported.active: Nothing approves a planning round. This chain is `issued`, so `active` does not resolve on it and is refused by name -- serving `latest` instead would answer 'what is in force' with a plan nobody put in force.

vintage.reason: An adoption is a coordinate on the vintage axis, not a filter. Every adoption the walk offers is already in the fact set, so switching is a re-selection of materialised values and not a new question. The report binds the SELECTOR `latest`; this control names the MEMBER that selector resolved to, because a member is the only part of the coordinate stable enough to reproduce or dispute.

period.label: Period
period.reason: Changing the period changes the period_frame coordinate of every measure in the spec. The plan calendarisation is resolved at refresh, not in the browser.

pisWindow.label: In-service window
pisWindow.reason: The window determines which months are record basis and which are projection. Widening it changes the basis mix, so the report re-resolves.
